```{r, include = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
options(width = 76)
# A figure whose pixels are all opaque is written without its alpha channel:
# the same pixels in a smaller file.
opaque_png <- function(path) {
  x <- png::readPNG(path)
  if (length(dim(x)) == 3 && dim(x)[3] == 4 && all(x[, , 4] == 1)) {
    png::writePNG(x[, , 1:3], path)
  }
  path
}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.4, out.width = "100%", dpi = 117,
                      fig.process = if (requireNamespace("png", quietly = TRUE)) opaque_png)
```

An array is scored on simulated animals, and the way they move changes the score. Figure 1 shows
one simulated animal under each of the five movement models of this page. Each section shows the
code that builds its model; sections 1, 2, 4 and 5 also walk its tracks, and the tracks of
section 3's model are walked in section 6.

```{r opening-one-animal-per-model, echo = FALSE, purl = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Five maps of parts of Stoney Lake, one simulated track each: a random walk wandering from the middle of the lake, a moving and resting track with squares where it rested, a track of resampled steps, a track running from the south-west arm to a goal on the north shore, and a track tangled over the deep north-east basin."}
# Run the code of sections 1 to 6 to draw Figure 1 first; the code is
# shown there
opening_chunks <- c("read-the-lake", "depth-map-helper",
                    "correlated-random-walk", "tracks-by-turning-spread",
                    "two-state-samplers", "two-state-model",
                    "two-state-track", "own-steps-sampler", "grid-array",
                    "release-and-goal", "head-for-a-goal", "depth-preference",
                    "walk-with-preference", "walk-three-preferences",
                    "score-by-movement-model")
opened <- eval(parse(text = unlist(knitr::knit_code$get(opening_chunks))))

# Take the first animal of one run of each model
model_panels <- c(crw = "(a) correlated random walk",
                  two_state = "(b) moving and resting",
                  own_steps = "(c) resampled steps",
                  goal = "(d) goal, bias 0.2",
                  habitat = "(e) prefers deep water")
model_runs <- list(crw = turn_tracks$forty, two_state = two_state,
                   own_steps = evaluations$own_steps$tracks,
                   goal = goal_tracks$a, habitat = preference_tracks$deep)
first_animals <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(model_runs), function(model) {
  run <- as.data.frame(model_runs[[model]])
  run <- run[run$path_id == run$path_id[1], ]
  data.frame(model = factor(model_panels[[model]], levels = model_panels),
             x = run$x, y = run$y, resting = run$state == 2)
}))
first_positions <- first_animals[!duplicated(first_animals$model), ]
goal_panel <- data.frame(goal, model = factor(model_panels[["goal"]],
                                              levels = model_panels))

# Zoom each panel to a square round its track, 600 m wider on each side, and
# take the water cells inside it
zoom_window <- function(track) {
  half <- max(diff(range(track$x)), diff(range(track$y))) / 2 + 600
  centre <- c(mean(range(track$x)), mean(range(track$y)))
  data.frame(model = track$model[1], x = centre[1] + c(-half, half),
             y = centre[2] + c(-half, half))
}
windows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(first_animals, first_animals$model),
                                 zoom_window))
water_inside <- function(window) {
  inside <- water$x >= min(window$x) & water$x <= max(window$x) &
    water$y >= min(window$y) & water$y <= max(window$y)
  data.frame(water[inside, ], model = window$model[1])
}
panel_water <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(windows, windows$model),
                                     water_inside))

# Give each panel the colour its model has in the later figures: the first
# animal of Figure 2, moving and resting as in Figure 3, goal bias 0.2 as in
# Figure 4 and the deep preference as in Figure 5
model_colours <- c(crw = "orange", two_state = "bluish_green",
                   own_steps = "blue", goal = "bluish_green",
                   habitat = "reddish_purple")
panel_colours <- c(setNames(model_colours[names(model_panels)], model_panels),
                   resting = "orange")

# Map one panel per model: the track over a white casing, the rests as
# squares, the start and the goal
ggplot(panel_water, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = depth_m)) +
  detfield::scale_fill_depth() +
  geom_blank(data = windows) +
  geom_path(data = first_animals, colour = "white", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_path(data = first_animals, aes(colour = model), linewidth = 0.45) +
  geom_point(data = first_animals[first_animals$resting, ],
             aes(colour = "resting"), shape = 15, size = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_tracks(colours = panel_colours, guide = "none") +
  geom_point(data = first_positions, shape = 21, fill = "white",
             colour = "black", size = 2, stroke = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = goal_panel, shape = 23, size = 2, stroke = 0.7,
             colour = "black", fill = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~model, ncol = 3, scales = "free") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  detfield::annotation_scale_bar(location = "br") +
  detfield::theme_positionr() +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1, axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.title = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        panel.grid = element_blank())
```

*Figure 1. The first simulated animal of a run of each model of sections 1 to 5 on Stoney Lake,
each panel zoomed to its track:
(a) 4 hours, (b) 8 hours, with squares where it rested, (c) 6 hours, (d) until it reached the
goal (diamond) after `r round(attr(goal_tracks$a, "arrived")[1] / 60, 1)` hours, and
(e) 48 hours. Circles mark the starts.*

This page sets the movement in five ways:

- a correlated random walk from three numbers;
- a switch between moving and resting, with step and turn distributions of your own, such as
  those of a hidden Markov model fitted to your species;
- a sampler of steps of your own, such as steps you measured;
- a start, a start time and a goal that pulls the animals towards it;
- a preference for a habitat layer, such as bottom depth, of a strength you set.

Each gives a movement model to pass to `simulate_tracks()` and `evaluate_array()`. Section 6
measures how much the choice changes an array's score. Its code installs as
`movement-models.R` in `system.file("scripts", package = "arraydesign")`.

Stoney Lake, Ontario, at 100 m resolution, is the example water body, as in
[Get started](arraydesign.html).
The first step loads the packages and reads the depth raster.

```{r read-the-lake}
# Load the package, and ggplot2 for the maps
library(arraydesign)
library(ggplot2)

# Read the depth raster of Stoney Lake
lake <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata", "stoney_depth.tif",
                                package = "arraydesign"))
```

Depth is zero or negative metres, so the maps take `abs()`. `depth_map()` is a page helper that
draws the water by depth, all of it or the part given by `zoom`.

```{r depth-map-helper}
# Take the water cells, with depth as positive metres
water <- terra::as.data.frame(lake, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)
names(water)[3] <- "depth_m"
water$depth_m <- abs(water$depth_m)

# Draw water by depth, land blank; `zoom` takes the x and y limits of a
# part of the lake, and NULL draws all of it
depth_map <- function(zoom = NULL) {
  ggplot(water, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_raster(aes(fill = depth_m)) +
    detfield::scale_fill_depth() +
    coord_equal(xlim = zoom$x, ylim = zoom$y, expand = FALSE) +
    labs(x = "Easting (m)", y = "Northing (m)") +
    detfield::annotation_scale_bar(location = "br") +
    detfield::theme_positionr()
}
```

## What a movement model holds

A movement model has four parts:

- a function that draws step lengths in metres;
- a function that draws turning angles in radians;
- the time one step takes, in seconds;
- a line saying where the numbers came from.

`simulate_tracks()` calls the two functions, turns the animal by the angle and moves it by the
step. A step that meets the shore is reflected off it, so no track crosses land. The source line
is printed with the model and kept with every simulation made from it.

## 1. A correlated random walk from three numbers

`crw_model()` takes step lengths from a gamma distribution with the mean and standard deviation
you give, per time step. It draws turning angles from a normal distribution centred on zero and
wrapped to the circle. A small turning spread gives straight paths; `turn_sd = Inf` gives a
walk with no memory of its heading. The walk of the
[**arraydesignR**](https://jakebrownscombe.github.io/arraydesignR/) R package, which runs
**arraydesign** in a browser, and of `evaluate_array()` moves a mean of 30 m a minute, 0.5 m/s, with turns of standard deviation 40
degrees. The print gives the model and its source line.

```{r correlated-random-walk}
# Build a walk: gamma steps of mean 30 m and sd 15 m per 60 s, turns of
# sd 40 degrees
walk <- crw_model(step_mean = 30, step_sd = 15, turn_sd = 40, time_step_s = 60)
walk
```

To see what steps the walk draws, the next chunk draws 10,000 of them and summarises their
lengths in metres.

```{r explore-step-lengths}
# Draw 10,000 step lengths from the walk, m per 60 s
set.seed(1)
step_draws <- walk$step(10000)
summary(step_draws)
```

The draws have a mean of `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(step_draws))` m and a median of
`r sprintf("%.1f", median(step_draws))` m; the long right tail of the gamma gives the odd step of
over `r floor(max(step_draws) / 50) * 50` m. These are starting values; no species was measured to set them. The next chunk releases five
animals together in the middle of the lake under three turning spreads: 10 degrees, 40 degrees
and uniform turns. `track_control(start = ...)` sets the release point; section 4 shows its other
settings.

```{r tracks-by-turning-spread}
# Set a release point in the middle of the lake
middle <- data.frame(x = 727850, y = 4937250)

# Set one turning spread per walk, in degrees; Inf gives uniform turns
turn_sds <- c(ten = 10, forty = 40, uniform = Inf)

# Walk five animals for 240 steps of 60 s under each walk
turn_tracks <- lapply(turn_sds, function(turn_sd) {
  spread_walk <- crw_model(step_mean = 30, step_sd = 15, turn_sd = turn_sd,
                           time_step_s = 60)
  simulate_tracks(lake, spread_walk, n_animals = 5, n_steps = 240,
                  control = track_control(start = middle), seed = 1)
})
```

At 10 degrees the animals travel long, straight paths, at 40 they wander, and with uniform turns
they stay near the release (Figure 2).

```{r map-turning-spread, fig.height = 5.6, fig.alt = "Three maps of Stoney Lake: tracks of five animals in five colours from one release point are long and straight at 10 degrees, wander at 40 degrees, and stay close to the release with uniform turns."}
# Name the panels, in the order of turn_sds
panel_names <- c(ten = "(a) 10 degrees", forty = "(b) 40 degrees",
                 uniform = "(c) uniform turns")

# Stack the three runs in one table, with the panel each is drawn in
spread_paths <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(turn_tracks), function(spread) {
  data.frame(path_id = turn_tracks[[spread]]$path_id,
             x = turn_tracks[[spread]]$x, y = turn_tracks[[spread]]$y,
             panel = panel_names[[spread]])
}))

# Draw one panel per turning spread over the middle of the lake, each
# track over a white casing
depth_map(zoom = list(x = c(724500, 731500), y = c(4934800, 4939800))) +
  geom_path(data = spread_paths, aes(group = path_id), colour = "white",
            linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_path(data = spread_paths, aes(group = path_id, colour = factor(path_id)),
            linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(data = middle, shape = 21, fill = "white", colour = "black",
             size = 2, stroke = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_tracks(name = "Animal") +
  facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 2) +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.75, 0.25),
        legend.box = "horizontal")
```

*Figure 2. Tracks of five simulated animals over 4 hours (240 steps of 60 s) released
together at one point (circle) in the middle of Stoney Lake, under a correlated random walk with
gamma steps of mean 30 m and standard deviation 15 m per minute and a turning-angle standard
deviation of (a) 10 degrees, (b) 40 degrees and (c) uniform turns.*

`attr(tracks, "escapes")` counts, per animal, the steps taken as drawn, reflected at the shore,
held in place, and still. A model whose steps are too long for the water body, or in the wrong units,
gives many reflections. `simulate_tracks()` warns when more than half of the moving steps were
reflected. Here are the counts of the run with uniform turns:

```{r count-shore-reflections}
# Count the steps per animal: as drawn, reflected, held and still
attr(turn_tracks$uniform, "escapes")
```

## 2. Moving and resting

Many animals alternate between moving and resting. `movement_model()` takes any pair of
samplers. With `states = 2` and a 2 by 2 transition matrix, the animal switches between moving
with the samplers (state 1) and staying in place (state 2). Rows are the state
at one step and columns the state at the next, so row 1 holds the probabilities of moving and of
resting after a moving step, and row 2 the same after a resting step; each row sums to 1. A
state kept with probability `p` (the diagonal) lasts a mean of `1 / (1 - p)` steps, which the
model prints.

A hidden Markov model fitted with the **moveHMM** or **momentuHMM** R package can have gamma step lengths and
wrapped Cauchy turning angles in its moving state. The wrapped Cauchy needs no extra package: a
Cauchy draw with scale `-log(rho)`, wrapped to the circle, has concentration `rho`. The values
below are illustrative values that no fit produced. Use the estimates of your own fit, in metres
per time step of that fit. The first chunk writes the two samplers.

```{r two-state-samplers}
# Set the moving-state estimates: mean and sd of step length (m per 60 s)
# and the concentration of the turning angles
hmm_step_mean <- 25
hmm_step_sd <- 15
hmm_rho <- 0.6

# Draw gamma step lengths with that mean and sd
gamma_steps <- function(n_draws) {
  stats::rgamma(n_draws, shape = (hmm_step_mean / hmm_step_sd)^2,
                rate = hmm_step_mean / hmm_step_sd^2)
}

# Draw wrapped Cauchy turning angles with concentration rho
wrapped_cauchy <- function(n_draws) {
  (stats::rcauchy(n_draws, 0, -log(hmm_rho)) + pi) %% (2 * pi) - pi
}
```

`movement_model()` joins the samplers, the time step and the transition matrix. The print gives
the mean time in each state.

```{r two-state-model}
# Set the transition matrix: rows are the state at one step, columns the
# state at the next (1 moving, 2 resting)
move_rest <- matrix(c(0.95, 0.05,    # moving: keep moving 0.95, rest 0.05
                      0.10, 0.90),   # resting: move 0.10, keep resting 0.90
                    nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)

# Move with the samplers (state 1) or rest (state 2)
hmm_model <- movement_model(
  step = gamma_steps, turn = wrapped_cauchy, time_step_s = 60,
  states = 2, transition = move_rest,
  source = paste("HMM, illustrative values: gamma steps 25 m (sd 15)",
                 "per 60 s, wrapped Cauchy turns rho 0.6, and rest")
)
hmm_model
```

`crw_model()` takes the same matrix for a correlated random walk that rests:
`crw_model(30, 15, 40, transition = move_rest)`. One animal walks
for 8 hours under the two-state model. The `state` column of the tracks gives the state of the
step that ends at each position, 1 moving and 2 resting.

```{r two-state-track}
# Walk one animal for 480 steps of 60 s from the middle of the lake
two_state <- simulate_tracks(lake, hmm_model, n_animals = 1, n_steps = 480,
                             control = track_control(start = middle), seed = 4)

# Count the positions in each state
table(two_state$state)
```

A resting animal stays where it is, so its resting positions fall at few places. The next chunk
counts them.

```{r resting-places}
# Take every position of the track, and those at which the animal rested
positions <- data.frame(x = two_state$x, y = two_state$y)
resting <- positions[two_state$state == 2, ]

# Count the resting positions, and the places at which the animal rested
nrow(resting)
nrow(unique(resting))
```

Over 8 hours the animal rested at `r nrow(resting)` of its `r nrow(two_state)` positions, at
`r nrow(unique(resting))` places (Figure 3).

```{r map-resting-positions, fig.alt = "One green track in the middle of Stoney Lake from a white start point, with orange squares where the animal rested."}
# Map the track over a white casing in the moving colour, the resting
# positions on top as squares in the resting colour, and the start, zoomed
# to the track
depth_map(zoom = list(x = range(two_state$x) + c(-800, 800),
                      y = range(two_state$y) + c(-800, 800))) +
  geom_path(data = positions, colour = "white", linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_path(data = positions, aes(colour = "Moving"), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = resting, aes(colour = "Resting"), shape = 15, size = 1.8) +
  geom_point(data = positions[1, ], shape = 21, fill = "white",
             colour = "black", size = 2.2, stroke = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_tracks(name = "State",
                      colours = c(Moving = "bluish_green", Resting = "orange")) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(linetype = c(1, 0),
                                                   shape = c(NA, 15))))
```

*Figure 3. Track of one simulated animal over 8 hours (480 steps of 60 s) from its start
(circle) under the two-state model: moving with gamma steps of mean 25 m per minute and
wrapped Cauchy turns (concentration 0.6) for a mean of 20 steps, then resting for a mean of 10
steps.*

## 3. A sampler of your own

The two functions can be anything that takes a number of draws, `n_draws`, and returns that many
numbers: step lengths of 0 or more, and turning angles in radians. One route is to resample steps you measured, such as the
distances between positions of your own tagged animals at a fixed interval. The twelve steps
below are example values; replace them with your own.

```{r own-steps-sampler}
# Enter twelve measured steps, m per 180 s
my_steps <- c(12, 34, 8, 56, 120, 44, 19, 73, 33, 251, 62, 28)

# Resample the steps; turn up to 90 degrees either way
own_model <- movement_model(
  step = function(n_draws) sample(my_steps, n_draws, replace = TRUE),
  turn = function(n_draws) stats::runif(n_draws, -pi / 2, pi / 2),
  time_step_s = 180,
  source = "twelve example steps per 180 s, resampled; turns up to 90 degrees"
)
own_model
```

`movement_model()` draws five values from each function before it returns. A sampler that gives
the wrong number of values, or a negative step, therefore stops it at once. A common error is to
draw one value where `n_draws` are needed:

```{r sampler-error}
# Try a step sampler that ignores n_draws and draws one value
try(movement_model(
  step = function(n_draws) stats::rgamma(1, shape = 2, rate = 0.1),
  turn = function(n_draws) stats::runif(n_draws, -pi, pi)
))
```

Use `n_draws` in every draw. `evaluate_array()` also needs a whole number of steps in an hour,
so the time step must divide 3600 s. To show the message, the next chunk sets up the 20-receiver
grid and the assumed range model of [Get started](arraydesign.html), which section 6 also uses.

```{r grid-array}
# Lay the 20-receiver grid of Get started over water at least 1 m deep
deployable <- terra::ifel(abs(lake) < 1, NA, lake)
receivers <- place_receivers(deployable, n = 20, method = "grid", seed = 1)

# Set the assumed range model: d50 and d05 for receivers 1 m and 35 m deep
range_model <- detfield::de_logistic(d50 = c(250, 750), d05 = c(500, 1500),
                                     depth = c(1, 35))
```

A walk with a step of seven minutes is refused:

```{r time-step-error}
# Build a walk with a time step of 420 s, which does not divide an hour
seven_minutes <- crw_model(step_mean = 210, step_sd = 105, turn_sd = 40,
                           time_step_s = 420)

# Try to evaluate it; evaluate_array() refuses it and names the fix
try(evaluate_array(receivers, lake, range_model,
                   control = list(movement = seven_minutes)))
```

Choose a time step such as 60, 120, 180, 300 or 600 s, and give the step lengths for that time
step.

## 4. Goal-oriented movement

By default each animal starts at the centre of a random water cell, at midnight UTC on
1 January 2025. `track_control()` sets the start positions and the start time. It can also add
a goal, such as a spawning site, that pulls every animal towards it:

- `goal`: one point on water;
- `goal_bias`: the weight of the bearing to the goal against the bearing of the walk, from 0,
  which ignores the goal, to 1, which heads straight for it;
- `goal_tolerance`: the distance at which an animal has arrived; it then stays at the goal.
  The default is one cell.

Here ten animals are released together in the south-west arm of the lake at 06:00 UTC on 1 June.
They move by the walk of section 1 towards a shallow bay on the north shore. An animal within
300 m of the goal has arrived. The first chunk sets the release, the goal and the start time.

```{r release-and-goal}
# Set a release point in the south-west arm and a goal on the north shore
release <- data.frame(x = 721950, y = 4930450)
goal <- data.frame(x = 725500, y = 4938000)
start_time <- as.POSIXct("2025-06-01 06:00:00", tz = "UTC")

# Compute the straight-line distance from the release to the goal, m
sqrt((goal$x - release$x)^2 + (goal$y - release$y)^2)
```

The goal is `r round(sqrt((goal$x - release$x)^2 + (goal$y - release$y)^2) / 1000, 1)` km from
the release in a straight line. The run is made at goal biases of 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5, for up to 24 hours each. The chunk returns
one set of tracks per bias and prints the time span of the first.

```{r head-for-a-goal}
# Set the goal biases to compare
biases <- c(a = 0.2, b = 0.3, c = 0.5)

# Walk ten animals for 1,440 steps of 60 s at each bias
goal_tracks <- lapply(biases, function(bias) {
  control <- track_control(start = release, goal = goal, goal_bias = bias,
                           goal_tolerance = 300, start_time = start_time)
  simulate_tracks(lake, walk, n_animals = 10, n_steps = 1440, control = control,
                  seed = 1)
})

# Print the first and last time of the run at a bias of 0.2
range(goal_tracks$a$time)
```

`arrived` gives the step at which each animal reached the goal, `NA` if it did not.

```{r arrival-steps}
# Take the step of arrival of each animal, at each bias
arrived <- lapply(goal_tracks, attr, "arrived")
arrived
```

With a goal bias of 0.2, all `r sum(!is.na(arrived$a))` animals arrive, after
`r round(min(arrived$a) / 60, 1)` to `r round(max(arrived$a) / 60, 1)` hours (Figure 4, panel a).

The pull acts on the heading only, so a strong pull can hold an animal against the shore where
the straight line to the goal crosses land. The check below asks how often that happened: the
share of moving steps reflected at the shore, at each bias.

```{r reflected-share}
# Compute the share of moving steps reflected at the shore, per bias
reflected_share <- sapply(goal_tracks, function(tracks) {
  escapes <- attr(tracks, "escapes")
  sum(escapes$reflected) / sum(escapes$clear, escapes$reflected, escapes$held)
})
round(reflected_share, 3)
```

At a bias of 0.3 all `r sum(!is.na(arrived$b))` animals still arrived and
`r round(100 * reflected_share[["b"]])`% of moving steps were reflected, against
`r round(100 * reflected_share[["a"]])`% at 0.2. At 0.5, `r sum(is.na(arrived$c))` of 10
animals were held on the shore and `r round(100 * reflected_share[["c"]])`% of moving steps were
reflected. On this lake, keep the bias at 0.3 or lower; where a goal lies behind a peninsula,
check `arrived` and the reflected share before you use a stronger pull.

```{r map-goal-tracks, fig.height = 4.2, fig.alt = "Three maps of the west half of Stoney Lake: tracks in green at a goal bias of 0.2, orange at 0.3 and purple at 0.5 run from a release point in the south-west arm to a goal on the north shore; at 0.5 some tracks stop against the shore short of the goal."}
# Draw a circle of 300 m round the goal, the arrival distance
angle <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 100)
arrival_ring <- data.frame(x = goal$x + 300 * cos(angle),
                           y = goal$y + 300 * sin(angle))

# Stack the tracks of the three biases, with the panel each is drawn in
bias_paths <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(biases), function(run) {
  data.frame(as.data.frame(goal_tracks[[run]])[c("path_id", "x", "y")],
             bias = as.character(biases[[run]]),
             panel = sprintf("(%s) goal bias %s", run, biases[[run]]))
}))

# Map the tracks over the west half of the lake, one panel and one colour
# per bias, each track over a white casing
goal_map <- depth_map(zoom = list(x = c(720300, 729500),
                                  y = c(4929240, 4939200))) +
  geom_path(data = bias_paths, aes(group = path_id), colour = "white",
            linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_path(data = bias_paths, aes(group = path_id, colour = bias),
            linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_tracks(name = "Goal bias",
                      colours = c("0.2" = "bluish_green", "0.3" = "orange",
                                  "0.5" = "reddish_purple")) +
  geom_point(data = release, shape = 21, fill = "white", colour = "black",
             size = 2, stroke = 0.6) +
  geom_path(data = arrival_ring, linetype = "dashed", colour = "black") +
  geom_point(data = goal, shape = 23, size = 2, stroke = 0.8,
             colour = "black", fill = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 3) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
goal_map
```

*Figure 4. Tracks of ten simulated animals over up to 24 hours (1,440 steps of 60 s), released
together (circle) in the south-west arm of Stoney Lake under the correlated random walk of
section 1 and pulled towards a goal in a bay on the north shore (diamond; dashed circle:
the 300 m arrival distance).*

A goal must lie in water that every start can reach through cells that share an edge;
`simulate_tracks()` stops otherwise. `evaluate_array()` releases its animals at random water
cells with no goal, and takes the start time as `control = list(start_time = ...)`.

## 5. A preference for a habitat layer

`habitat_selection()` gives a movement model a preference for the values of a raster layer.
Each step is drawn from the walk of section 1 and kept with probability proportional to
`exp(beta * layer)` at its end; a step not kept is drawn again. The animals therefore select the
layer with a strength `beta` per unit at the scale of one step, known exactly, and a simulated
study becomes a test of whether a habitat analysis recovers a preference that is known. Here the
layer is bottom depth, and `beta = -0.3` per m favours shallow water.

```{r depth-preference}
# Make a layer of bottom depth in positive metres, named for the analysis
depth <- abs(lake)
names(depth) <- "depth_m"

# Give the walk of section 1 a preference for shallow water: a log weight
# of -0.3 per m of bottom depth
shallow_walk <- habitat_selection(walk, depth, beta = -0.3)
shallow_walk
```

Twenty animals walk for 48 hours from 20 water cells drawn once. The print counts the candidate
steps drawn and the steps kept; `attr(shallow_tracks, "selection")` gives the same counts per
animal.

```{r walk-with-preference}
# Draw 20 release cells on water, used for every run of this section
set.seed(20)
releases <- water[sample(nrow(water), 20), c("x", "y")]

# Walk 20 animals for 2,880 steps of 60 s (48 hours) from those cells
shallow_tracks <- simulate_tracks(lake, shallow_walk, n_animals = 20,
                                  n_steps = 2880,
                                  control = track_control(start = releases),
                                  seed = 1)
shallow_tracks
```

The next chunk walks five of these animals, the first five released in the eastern part of the
lake (east of 727,000 m and north of 4,935,600 m: the north-east basin and the east of the
central lake), under three preferences: for shallow water, none, and for deep water (`beta = 0.3`). It prints
the median bottom depth of each run's positions.

```{r walk-three-preferences}
# Take the first five releases in the eastern part of the lake, the area
# of Figure 5, which holds the north-east basin and the deepest water
basin <- list(x = c(727000, 737400), y = c(4935600, 4941900))
basin_releases <- releases[releases$x > basin$x[1] &
                             releases$y > basin$y[1], ][1:5, ]

# Set three preferences for bottom depth, per m
betas <- c(shallow = -0.3, none = 0, deep = 0.3)

# Walk the five animals for 48 hours under each preference
preference_tracks <- lapply(betas, function(beta) {
  simulate_tracks(lake, habitat_selection(walk, depth, beta = beta),
                  n_animals = 5, n_steps = 2880,
                  control = track_control(start = basin_releases), seed = 1)
})

# Median bottom depth of the positions of each run, m
depth_values <- terra::values(depth, mat = FALSE)
used_depth <- sapply(preference_tracks, function(tracks) {
  median(depth_values[tracks$cell])
})
round(used_depth, 2)
```

From the same five releases, the animals that favour shallow water keep to the margins of the
basin and skirt its deep hole, and those that favour deep water gather over it (Figure 5).

```{r map-three-preferences, fig.height = 5.6, fig.alt = "Three maps of the eastern part of Stoney Lake with the tracks of five simulated animals from the same release points, orange for shallow, green for no preference and purple for deep: with a preference for shallow water the tracks avoid the deep hole, with none they cross it, and with a preference for deep water they gather over it."}
# Name the panels, in the order of betas
preference_names <- c(shallow = "(a) beta -0.3 per m, shallow",
                      none = "(b) beta 0, no preference",
                      deep = "(c) beta 0.3 per m, deep")

# Stack the three runs, with the panel each is drawn in
preference_paths <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  names(preference_tracks),
  function(run) {
    data.frame(path_id = preference_tracks[[run]]$path_id,
               x = preference_tracks[[run]]$x, y = preference_tracks[[run]]$y,
               preference = run, panel = preference_names[[run]])
  }
))

# Draw one panel and one colour per preference over the eastern part of
# the lake, each track over a white casing
depth_map(zoom = basin) +
  geom_path(data = preference_paths, aes(group = path_id), colour = "white",
            linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_path(data = preference_paths,
            aes(group = path_id, colour = preference), linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(data = basin_releases, shape = 21, fill = "white",
             colour = "black", size = 1.6, stroke = 0.5) +
  scale_colour_tracks(name = "Preference",
                      colours = c(shallow = "orange", none = "bluish_green",
                                  deep = "reddish_purple"),
                      breaks = names(betas),
                      labels = c("prefers shallow", "no preference",
                                 "prefers deep")) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 2) +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.75, 0.25),
        legend.box = "horizontal")
```

*Figure 5. Tracks of five simulated animals over 48 hours (2,880 steps of 60 s)
from the same five release points (circles) in the eastern part of Stoney Lake, the
north-east basin and the east of the central lake, under
the correlated random walk of section 1 with a preference for bottom depth of (a) -0.3 per m,
(b) none and (c) 0.3 per m. Tracks that leave the basin are cut at the edge of the map.*

`available_steps()` checks the truth on the tracks themselves. For each step an animal took it
draws 10 control steps from the same walk, from the same start and heading, and reads the depth
at each end. A conditional logit of the step taken against its controls estimates `beta`; the
**survival** R package fits it.

```{r draw-available-steps}
# Draw 10 control steps for each step of the 20 animals
shallow_steps <- available_steps(shallow_tracks, n = 10, seed = 2)
head(shallow_steps)
```

The model is fitted to each animal on its own, so the animal is the replicate.

```{r fit-per-animal}
# Attach survival; clogit() reads a bare strata() term
library(survival)

# Fit a conditional logit per animal: step taken (case 1) against controls
per_animal <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(shallow_steps, shallow_steps$path_id),
  function(steps) {
    fit <- clogit(case ~ depth_m + strata(stratum), data = steps)
    data.frame(path_id = steps$path_id[1], estimate = unname(coef(fit)),
               se = sqrt(unname(diag(vcov(fit)))))
  }
))
head(per_animal)
```

The next chunk sets the mean of the 20 estimates, with a 95% interval from their spread, against
the `beta` of the model, and counts the animals whose own 95% interval holds it.

```{r compare-with-beta}
# Mean across animals and its 95% interval, t on 19 degrees of freedom
mean_estimate <- mean(per_animal$estimate)
half_width <- qt(0.975, 19) * sd(per_animal$estimate) / sqrt(20)
round(c(beta = -0.3, mean = mean_estimate,
        lower = mean_estimate - half_width,
        upper = mean_estimate + half_width), 3)

# Count the animals whose 95% interval holds beta
covered <- sum(abs(per_animal$estimate + 0.3) <=
                 qnorm(0.975) * per_animal$se)
covered
```

The 20 animals give a mean of `r sprintf("%.3f", mean_estimate)` per m (95% interval
`r sprintf("%.3f", mean_estimate - half_width)` to `r sprintf("%.3f", mean_estimate + half_width)`)
against the -0.3 of the model, and the intervals of `r covered` of 20 animals hold -0.3. The
coefficient holds at the scale of one step. A fit to positions an hour apart compares places
farther apart, so it need not return the same number; test it against a fit to the true track at
that scale.

## 6. How much the movement model changes the score

The 20-receiver grid is scored with the example's assumed range model and the reference run of
**arraydesignR** (20 animals for 6 hours, a delay of 120 to 180 s) under four movement models: a slow walk of 6 m a minute, the walk of section 1, the
two-state model of section 2, and the resampled steps of section 3. The chunk returns one
evaluation per model.

```{r score-by-movement-model, message = FALSE}
# Build a slow walk: 6 m a minute
slow_walk <- crw_model(step_mean = 6, step_sd = 4, turn_sd = 40,
                       time_step_s = 60)

# Name the four movement models
models <- list(slow = slow_walk, crw = walk, two_state = hmm_model,
               own_steps = own_model)

# Evaluate the grid under each
evaluations <- lapply(models, function(model) {
  evaluate_array(receivers, lake, range_model, n_animals = 20,
                 seed = 1,
                 control = list(hours = 6, tag_delay = c(120, 180),
                                movement = model))
})
```

The next chunk tabulates the detection rate of each animal under each model.

```{r rate-per-animal}
# Tabulate the detection rate, one row per model and animal
rates <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(evaluations), function(model) {
  sent <- evaluations[[model]]$detections$transmissions
  rate <- tapply(sent$n_detections > 0, sent$path_id, mean)
  data.frame(movement = model, animal_id = names(rate),
             rate = as.vector(rate))
}))
head(rates)
```

The table summarises them per model, beside the positioning error and the hit rate.

```{r compare-the-models}
# Tabulate detection, positioning error and hit rate, one row per model
by_model <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(evaluations), function(model) {
  overall <- evaluations[[model]]$score$overall
  model_rates <- rates$rate[rates$movement == model]
  data.frame(movement = model, mean_rate = round(mean(model_rates), 3),
             never_heard = sum(model_rates == 0),
             median_error_m = round(overall$median_error_mean_m),
             hit_rate = round(overall$hit_rate, 3))
}))
by_model
```

The slow walk leaves `r by_model$never_heard[by_model$movement == "slow"]` of 20 animals
never heard, against `r by_model$never_heard[by_model$movement == "crw"]` under the walk of
30 m a minute (Figure 6). A slow animal that starts far from a receiver may never come within
range in six hours, while one that starts near a receiver is heard often.

```{r plot-rate-by-movement-model, fig.height = 3.8, fig.alt = "Detection rate per animal under four movement models; the two-state model leaves the most animals never heard, and the slow walk and the resampled steps tie behind it."}
# Name each model in words on the axis
model_names <- c(slow = "walk, 6 m a minute", crw = "walk, 30 m a minute",
                 two_state = "move and rest", own_steps = "resampled steps")
rates$movement <- factor(model_names[rates$movement], levels = model_names)

# Compute the mean rate per model, to draw as a bar
means <- aggregate(rate ~ movement, data = rates, FUN = mean)

# Draw one point per animal, spread sideways, and the mean per model
ggplot(rates, aes(movement, rate)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, seed = 1),
             colour = "#21908C", alpha = 0.7, size = 1.6) +
  geom_errorbar(data = means, aes(ymin = rate, ymax = rate), width = 0.4,
                colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(share) sprintf("%g%%", 100 * share),
                     limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Movement model", y = "Share of transmissions heard") +
  detfield::theme_positionr()
```

*Figure 6. Share of transmissions heard by at least one receiver of the 20-receiver grid
for each of 20 simulated animals over 6 hours, under four movement models: a slow correlated
random walk of 6 m a minute, the walk of 30 m a minute of section 1, the two-state model of
section 2, and the resampled example steps of section 3. Bars mark the mean across animals. All
four runs release the animals at the same 20 points.*

The hit rate is
`r sprintf("%.3f", by_model$hit_rate[by_model$movement == "crw"])` for the walk of 30 m a
minute and `r sprintf("%.3f", by_model$hit_rate[by_model$movement == "slow"])` for 6 m a
minute. The location surface for
an hour assumes the animal stayed in one place, so the 95% regions of faster animals hold the
truth less often.

Score a design with a movement model as close to your species as you can set, and with a slower
and a faster one beside it, to see how far the result depends on the choice.
